en: The people who sought her died,
And warriors of many tribes died.
Those who went were swept by a black wind;
No human being could match such might.
Kayypchal’s valiant daughter,
A maiden who brings strife to the whole world,
A maiden seasoned in bloody battle,
Gave true punishment
To every person who fought her.
Her arms and armor numbered eighty-four;
Where she struck, red fire flared.
She brought the whole world under her sway;
In all creation there cannot be
Another calamity like her.
Her father was Kayypchal,
And his people were said to be wicked.
The warrior’s homeland
Was a place called Jelpиниsh.
Her father was a khan who died;
A woman in name but a lion in truth,
She caused extraordinary turmoil.
She was a fiercely glowing ember;
Among all the sons born to mankind
There was no champion like her.
Her father was rich in people.
Her fortune was perfectly full,
Her pegs were made of steel,
And all her worldly goods stood ready.
Fortunate Kayypchal
Possessed every treasure he desired.
Fifteen tigers guarded her path;
No person dared approach,
And no enemy who met them prevailed.
Her gate was narrow,
And against the world that stormed it
She held such dreadful wonders.
Looking beyond it,
One saw a path meant for the young.
She had trained herself thoroughly:
With one blow she destroyed,
When enemies appeared she overturned them,
And those who provoked her wrath
She uprooted utterly.
She has an elephant with a sword-like trunk,
And until Judgment Day
It seems it cannot be captured—
Know this, my poor lady.
This is what Ajybay has seen;
If you are wise, heed my words.
No person has approached
That fortunate, ill-starred woman,
And none who met her survived.
When I looked upon that farther side,
My heart leapt from its place;
When I counted all her deeds,
My arms came out of their sockets,
And my heart burst from its casing.
Every bone in me shook,
And my fly-sized soul shrieked.
Who could love her so greatly
As simply to despair of life?
I struggled for my very soul,
And nearly abandoned life.
The reason for my despair was this:
Many giants and ogres had come,
Yet he did not heed what they said
And would not give them his valiant daughter.
Farther on stands a golden throne,
Surrounded by a grove of plane trees.
There is a path wide enough for one soul,
And beside it lies a deeply dug pit;
That God-stricken woman
Seems ready to trample all who pass.
There is a creature called the man-eater,
As large as an elephant’s head,
Which sucks human beings dry;
And there is a scorpion called Salagün.
There are many such accursed things.
May no living mortal see
The torment I have seen;
May it never befall another soul.
I endured such cruel affliction
That only a spoonful of blood remained,
And my flesh became a blue pulp.
My Karager grew thin as a twig,
And I myself became small as a lark.
When I surveyed that calamity
And cast my eyes beyond,
Something inhaled from six ravines away:
The dragon-serpent Karamar,
Which swallows whatever it encounters,
And bathes in blood when challenged—
How could any person face it?
With costly venom and a merciless nature,
Could I gain any news
Of the frenzied bride who treads the hours?
If one challenges this ill-starred outcast,
Could anyone remain alive?
Would any man survive being caught by it?
Would one who met it ever return alive?
Who could encounter it and say,
‘Let this bride be ours;
Come and accept our hospitality’?
Truth and falsehood became plain,
And I despaired of my fly-sized soul;
The hero himself despaired of life.
Her bearing and her majesty
Surpassed everything in the world—
Such was that infidel’s ordeal.
When I looked to this nearer side,
My heart leapt from its place;
When I counted all her deeds,
Before the khan stood a tower—
Ask me nothing of that tower.
Its hellish chamber was vast as a mountain;
To look upon it was calamity itself.
The tower had a doorway,
But its opening was misshapen.
It had gates at six places,
And at each gate an old keeper.
Her violence surpassed all bounds;
In countless forms appeared
The warriors of that infidel.
The gate doors were made of steel,
And keepers stood at every gate.
Frightened into submission by her appearance,
They wore human noses and ears
Strung about them as amulets.
Whenever they heard the maiden’s command,
They attacked at once.
When they grappled with those who sought her,
The seekers’ blood was spilled.
Such was the valor displayed
By Kayypchal’s warrior daughter.
That perfectly formed, ill-starred woman—
Could even a skillful man subdue her?
If many warriors attacked,
Could any man force her to bow?
Would anyone dare journey there?
After challenging that wrathful figure,
Could anyone survive?
Would any person confront
That dark, ill-starred fiend,
That sinister and accursed one?
Could renowned heroes subdue her?
Her waist is strong and her venom fierce;
Could anyone face and defeat her?
Could anyone who faced
That vicious-tempered warrior return alive?
From the hands of that merciless woman,
Could a mortal return alive to his people?
Once, wearing a blue-lynx and sable hat,
When I rode proudly along,
And among the people my carriage
Was rolling on its way,
I never yielded
Or stepped aside from the straight road.
When I sought what I desired,
I served as mediator before khans,
Going freely among them.
In the narrow passages of the wide world,
While the lion-hearted noble lived,
Where even a surging flood could not enter
And no attacking man could reach,
I went to Bakburchu of Kambal Khan,
Out upon his plain.
Through the gate where the khan was fortified,
In the narrow passages of the wide world,
While generous Manas,
The youngest of six lions, still lived,
When death was shared amid the tumult,
And among the people of forty tribes
The dear hero still lived unharmed,
When one or two great fortunes
Were flourishing,
I bore a golden shield and spear
And rode proudly,
Rejoicing before
The generous khan.
To the plane-tree garden of the Khagan,
To Khan Esen’s throne,
I went as an envoy.
I then petitioned for
Khan Esen’s golden throne.
I did not flinch or lose heart,
Nor did I suffer the least distress.
Nowhere on the face of the earth
Have I seen suffering like today’s.
Though death might come and my days end,
I did not die for Kuyaly.
Never while alive have I seen
A calamity like this,
Because of deeds long past,
Because of this lady,
Because of her fortress high as a craggy mountain,
And because ancestral spirits stand between us.
How can I go to that fierce-tempered
Warrior maiden, saying,
‘I will bring this matter before her people’?
That warrior maiden is a hero,
An infidel who lays nations waste,
Yet she is a broad-hearted soul,
Slender-waisted beneath her red dress,
A graceful beauty.”
Knowing secrets from the cast of her mind,
Such was that graceful warrior.
Her own words were sweet as sugar,
And her gazelle eyes shone brightly.
She was slender as willow silk,
Her eyes set like a young camel’s.
She had black, kohl-darkened brows
And long, flowing raven hair.
Her speech was marvelous;
She alone had been created
With beauty such as this.
She was gifted and gracious with people,
Her nature lovely, her speech honey,
And every word she spoke was sweet.
Sixty young wives and eighty maidens
Shared in her pleasures,
Slept within one palace,
And told each other their inmost secrets.
So many souls formed her retinue;
Among the warrior maiden’s attendants
Was a beautiful lady.
She was the light of sparkling eyes,
The fairest of the attendant maidens,
The most eloquent of living girls,
The ablest of humankind.
To the moonlike, beautiful maiden,
To that exalted one unlike other mortals,
To that infidel, vigilant and prepared,
She could unravel the knot of any matter,
A poised and open-hearted woman.
Bowing his massive head into his hands,
Ajybay of the Argyn khans
Humbled his khanly head
And sent an interpreter between them;
Through Janak I received the news.
Crossing passes and treading over stones,
Thinking deeply and grieving much,
Wearing out the gray racehorse,
Withering and aging my soul,
I journeyed forth utterly alone,
Folding up my coat of chain mail,
Exhausting my precious life
And wearing out every racehorse,
Turning them all and training them,
Until every provision was spent,
I traversed the entire world.
Through the world’s four corners
I traveled four full circuits.
When you wear out horses upon the road
And spend your blood to gain an answer,
You reach at last the appointed place.
I am an envoy who has come between you;
